analysis.one_liner: Sets the first federal rulebook for crypto, splitting oversight between the SEC and CFTC.
analysis.headline: Despite a bipartisan launch and three Senate hearings, the bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create the first comprehensive federal framework for digital assets. It would split oversight between the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, put most tokens under the CFTC's lighter-touch regime, let crypto exchanges register with the CFTC, and let banks issue dollar-backed stablecoins held to 100% reserves. It would also give tax breaks to crypto users and miners and add consumer protections like segregated customer funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Crypto companies gain most: exchanges would get a CFTC registration path instead of facing SEC securities enforcement, and tokens sold alongside investment contracts would be presumed commodities rather than securities once issuers met disclosure requirements. Crypto miners and stakers would defer income tax until they sell their coins. Banks would gain a new line of business issuing stablecoins. Ordinary crypto users would get modest benefits: no tax on small purchases with gains of $200 or less, segregated customer funds at registered exchanges, and clearer tax rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Crypto firms, exchanges, miners, and banks

how_it_helps.text: Divides jurisdiction over digital assets between the SEC, which keeps securities, and the CFTC, which would get most other tokens, and lets digital asset exchanges register directly with the CFTC, ending the uncertainty over which regulator applies.

Presumes that tokens sold alongside investment contracts are commodities, not securities, once the issuer meets semiannual disclosure requirements, which would shield most token issuers from securities-law liability and litigation risk.
Allows depository institutions to issue payment stablecoins, requiring them to hold reserves equal to 100% of outstanding coins and redeem them one-for-one for dollars.

Adds consumer protections: registered exchanges and futures merchants must segregate customer money and assets, are barred from commingling them with house funds, and must follow disclosure, anti-manipulation, and market-surveillance standards.
Gives tax relief to crypto users: no income tax on purchases using virtual currency that produce $200 or less in gain, and mining and staking rewards are not taxed until the coins are sold.
Orders studies and reports on energy use of digital asset mining, decentralized finance, retirement investing in crypto, and cybersecurity standards for intermediaries.

analysis.who_pays: The SEC would cede primary jurisdiction over most tokens to the CFTC, which historically polices futures markets and has far less authority and fewer resources for cash markets, leaving retail investors with thinner protections against fraud in spot trading. The Treasury would lose a modest amount of revenue from the tax deferrals and the $200 exclusion. Crypto buyers would give up the ability to sue under securities laws for most tokens, and the public would bear the risk if the stablecoin and CFTC framework proved inadequate in a crisis.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail investors, SEC jurisdiction, and federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill moves most tokens out of securities law and into the CFTC's jurisdiction; the CFTC oversees futures markets and has traditionally had much less power over cash trading, so everyday crypto buyers would have weaker anti-fraud protection than stock investors do.
Customers could waive the fund-segregation protections in writing, which would let exchanges pool customer assets with their consent and recreate exactly the risk the rule was meant to prevent.

The tax provisions, including the $200 exclusion and the deferral of tax on mining and staking income until sale, primarily benefit active crypto traders, miners, and stakers, at a cost to federal revenue.

Once an issuer meets the disclosure requirements, its token is presumed a commodity, and even an issuer that fails to comply is not thereby treated as selling a security, limiting investors' recourse under securities laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real gains: genuine regulatory clarity after years of uncertainty, 100%-reserved stablecoins, segregated customer funds, and modest tax relief for small users. But the framework is drawn largely to the industry's preference: the friendlier regulator gets most tokens, issuers escape securities liability, miners and stakers defer taxes, and customers can opt out of key protections. An honest supporter would acknowledge that investor protection was traded away to win industry agreement, and the consumer safeguards never would have made up for lighter spot-market oversight.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee when introduced, the Banking Committee held three hearings on it, and it never got a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cynthia Lummis introduced the bill on June 7, 2022 for herself and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a Republican-Democratic pairing; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, presumably because of its tax provisions.
One additional Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill, and the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee held hearings on it on July 28, September 15, and November 15, 2022.
The Finance Committee, the committee of referral, never reported the bill; it received no markup, no floor vote, and no House action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, crypto firms got neither the CFTC-centered rulebook nor the tax breaks they sought, and the SEC kept its broader enforcement authority over tokens; but ordinary crypto users also gained none of the bill's custody, stablecoin, and small-purchase tax protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crypto firms got nothing; SEC authority stood

sides.party_line_note: The bill was written and introduced jointly by a Wyoming Republican and a New York Democrat and picked up one more Democratic cosponsor; no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would give exchanges a CFTC registration path and presume most tokens are commodities rather than securities, freeing issuers from securities-law liability. In exchange they would take on disclosure, custody-segregation, and anti-manipulation obligations, but under a regulator with a much lighter touch on spot markets.

Banks would win the right to issue payment stablecoins, a lucrative business collecting dollar deposits and earning return on 100% reserves. The requirement to back every coin one-for-one and redeem on demand protects the people holding them.
Mining and staking rewards would not be taxed until the coins are sold, a major cash-flow benefit to an energy- and capital-intensive industry, at a modest cost to federal revenue.

The SEC would cede primary jurisdiction over most digital assets to the CFTC, keeping only securities and issuer disclosure. Its loss is concentrated institutional power, but its enforcement reach is what retail investors currently rely on against token fraud.
